reference.source: Resnick Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
clinicalPearls: Condensing osteitis of the clavicle is a benign, non-infective sclerosis of the medial clavicle, typically in women of childbearing age.
It presents with localised pain and sometimes swelling over the medial clavicle near the sternoclavicular joint, aggravated by shoulder movement.
Radiographs show sclerosis and mild expansion of the inferomedial clavicle with preservation of the sternoclavicular joint space and no bony destruction.
The absence of joint erosion, periostitis and soft-tissue mass distinguishes it from infection and malignancy.
It is thought to reflect a chronic stress or mechanical reaction of the medial clavicle rather than an inflammatory or infective arthropathy.
CT best demonstrates the sclerosis and confirms an intact cortex and joint, while MRI may show marrow oedema during painful phases.
It must be differentiated from SAPHO syndrome and sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis, which cause more florid hyperostosis and often skin lesions.
Management is conservative with analgesia and reassurance, and symptoms commonly settle over time.
reference.pathophysiology: Condensing osteitis of the clavicle is regarded as a reactive sclerosing process of the medial clavicle, probably driven by chronic mechanical stress across the sternoclavicular region, which is subject to considerable load during upper limb and shoulder use. Repetitive stress is thought to provoke increased osteoblastic activity and trabecular thickening of the inferomedial clavicular bone, producing dense sclerosis without the cortical destruction, sequestration or periosteal reaction seen in infection, and without the neoplastic matrix of a bone tumour. The condition is not associated with an identifiable organism or systemic inflammatory disorder, and its self-limiting course supports a mechanical rather than infective or autoimmune aetiology.
additionalDifferentials: Friedrich disease (osteonecrosis of the medial clavicle)
osteoblastic metastasis or primary bone tumour
additionalInvestigations: plain radiography of the clavicle and sternoclavicular joint
CT to confirm sclerosis with intact cortex and joint space
MRI to assess marrow oedema and exclude a soft-tissue mass
bone scintigraphy to gauge activity and screen for multifocal disease
inflammatory markers to help exclude infection and SAPHO
biopsy reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain lesions
redFlags: fever, warmth and rising inflammatory markers suggesting sternoclavicular infection
destructive or expansile change with a soft-tissue mass indicating tumour
palmoplantar pustulosis or acne pointing to SAPHO syndrome
progressive symptoms or atypical imaging warranting biopsy
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, with symptoms typically resolving or becoming quiescent over months to years and no risk of malignant change.
pitfalls: Mistaking the sclerosis for osteoblastic metastasis and pursuing an oncological work-up.
Overlooking sternoclavicular infection, which can present similarly but requires urgent treatment.
Failing to screen for the skin lesions and multifocal bone involvement of SAPHO syndrome.
Performing unnecessary biopsy of a radiologically characteristic benign lesion.
Confusing it with Friedrich disease, which is osteonecrosis rather than reactive sclerosis.
references: Resnick Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders, current edition
Taybi and Lachman Radiology of Syndromes, Metabolic Disorders and Skeletal Dysplasias
management: Reassure the patient about the benign, self-limiting nature of the condition, since it resolves over months to years without malignant potential
Manage conservatively with activity and load modification, avoiding aggravating overhead and shoulder-loading activity
Provide symptomatic relief with simple analgesics or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs during painful phases
Use physiotherapy to maintain shoulder movement and function
Observe with clinical and imaging follow-up to confirm stability, reserving biopsy for atypical or diagnostically uncertain lesions
Exclude infection and the SAPHO syndrome where inflammatory features or multifocal disease are present
Consider surgical excision only for persistent, disabling pain unresponsive to conservative measures
